result: Cell-type-specific variation in the requirement for forminCYK-1, but not myosin-IINMY-2, was identified in four-cell C. elegans embryos. ABa and ABp cells are sensitive to forminCYK-1 inactivation, failing cytokinesis at restrictive temperatures, while EMS and P2 cells are resistant, successfully completing cytokinesis even at 26-27°C where ABa/ABp always fail.
evaluation: Claims C47-C83 are supported by systematic temperature-shift experiments (Figure 1) showing differential cytokinesis outcomes across blastomeres. The data demonstrate that myosin-II inactivation causes similar failure rates in all four cells, while forminCYK-1 inactivation shows clear cell-type specificity with quantitative measurements at multiple temperatures. The experimental design includes appropriate controls and sufficient sample sizes (n≥5-81 per condition).

result: Temporal requirement analysis reveals that myosin-IINMY-2 is required throughout cytokinesis in all four blastomeres, while forminCYK-1 shows cell-type-specific temporal requirements. ABa requires forminCYK-1 throughout cytokinesis, ABp requires it only early, and EMS/P2 have lower overall requirements with successful division even when upshifted before anaphase onset.
evaluation: Claims C84-C95 are supported by temporal upshift experiments (Figure 2) with temperature shifts at defined times relative to anaphase onset. The data show clear differences in temporal sensitivity between cell types with adequate sample sizes (n≥57-79 per condition). The conclusion that forminCYK-1-mediated actin dynamics underlie cytokinetic diversity (C95) is a reasonable inference from the combined functional and temporal data.

result: EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption at restrictive temperature, yet still show considerable equatorial constriction and successful cytokinesis. This suggests these cells are less dependent on robust F-actin in the contractile ring and utilize cell-type-specific mechanisms for division.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C110-C115 are supported by F-actin imaging data using multiple reporters (Lifeact::RFP, PLST-1::GFP, GFP::UtrophinABD) shown in Figures 4 and supplements. The data demonstrate loss of F-actin enrichment at the contractile ring in all cells at 26°C in formincyk-1(ts) mutants, including in EMS/P2 cells that successfully divide. The inference that cell-type-specific mechanisms allow division without robust F-actin (C115) is well-supported by the combined observations.

result: Pharmacological inhibition of F-actin polymerization with LatrunculinA phenocopies the cell-type-specific requirement for forminCYK-1. ABa and ABp cells are sensitive to LatA treatment, while EMS and P2 cells are resistant, dividing at higher frequencies at the same LatA concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 and C116-C120 are supported by LatA dose-response experiments (Figure 5) showing cell-specific effects. At 80 nM LatA, 100% of ABa/ABp cells fail while ~25% of EMS/P2 cells successfully divide. This independent validation using a different perturbation method strengthens the conclusion that EMS/P2 are protected against cytokinesis failure when F-actin is weakened. Sample sizes are adequate (n=13-21 per condition).

result: Blastomere isolation experiments reveal that P2 cytokinesis is cell-intrinsically regulated, maintaining protection against forminCYK-1 disruption when isolated (~30% success rate). In contrast, EMS cytokinesis is cell-extrinsically regulated, with isolated EMS cells always failing cytokinesis (0/22 success) despite succeeding ~33% of the time in intact embryos.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C121-C130 are supported by blastomere isolation experiments (Figure 6) with clear quantitative outcomes. The experimental design appropriately tests intrinsic vs. extrinsic regulation by removing cell-cell contacts. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-26 per condition). The conclusion that P2 is intrinsically protected while EMS requires extrinsic signals is well-supported by the differential outcomes upon isolation.

result: Blastomere pairing experiments demonstrate that direct cell-cell contact from P2 is sufficient to restore cytokinetic protection in EMS. EMS cells paired with P2 divide successfully 16% of the time, while isolated EMS or EMS paired with ABd never divide. Increased EMS-P2 contact area correlates with successful EMS division, suggesting a link between P2-to-EMS signaling and cytokinetic protection.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 and C131-C140 are supported by blastomere pairing experiments (Figure 7) showing specific rescue of EMS cytokinesis by P2 contact. The correlation between contact area and division success (C137: p=0.0266) provides quantitative support, though the sample size for successful divisions is small (n=5). The inference of a correlation between signaling and division (C140) is reasonable but remains correlative rather than mechanistic.

result: EMS spindle orientation, a marker of successful P2-to-EMS signaling, correlates with cytokinesis outcome in formincyk-1(ts) mutants. In control EMS-P2 doublets, EMS spindles always align with the doublet axis (~180°). In formincyk-1(ts) doublets, only 48% show proper alignment, but all EMS cells that successfully divide (5/5) have properly aligned spindles. P2 cytokinesis outcome is independent of EMS spindle orientation.
evaluation: Claims C141-C148 are supported by spindle orientation analysis in paired blastomeres (Figure 8C). The data show clear correlation between proper spindle alignment and successful EMS division in formincyk-1(ts) mutants. The observation that all dividing EMS cells have proper alignment (5/5) is compelling despite small sample size. The independence of P2 outcomes from EMS spindle orientation supports cell-intrinsic regulation in P2. The suggestion of forminCYK-1 involvement in P2-EMS signaling (C145) is speculative but reasonable.

result: Cytokinesis in EMS is dependent on SrcSRC-1 signaling. RNAi depletion of SrcSRC-1 in formincyk-1(ts) embryos specifically decreases successful division in EMS (2/46 vs. 21/65 in controls) while not affecting P2 division frequency (22/50 vs. 29/77 in controls). SrcSRC-1 depletion has no effect in non-ts control embryos.
evaluation: Claims C61 and C149-C152 are supported by SrcSRC-1 RNAi experiments (Figure 8D and supplement). The data show specific reduction in EMS cytokinesis success upon SrcSRC-1 depletion in the sensitized formincyk-1(ts) background, with no effect on P2 or in wild-type embryos. Sample sizes are adequate (n=29-77 per condition). This provides strong evidence that the extrinsic mechanism protecting EMS depends on SrcSRC-1 signaling.

result: ForminCYK-1::eGFP localizes to the division plane in all four blastomeres with similar peak cortical levels (maximum intensity projection). Sum intensity projection shows reduced total levels in EMS and P2 compared to ABa/ABp, but this does not support the hypothesis that resistance to forminCYK-1 inactivation is due to protein enrichment in EMS/P2.
evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by imaging of endogenous forminCYK-1::eGFP (Figure 3 and supplements). The maximum intensity projection data clearly show similar peak levels across all cells, while sum projection shows lower total levels in EMS/P2. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations of sum projection analysis in multicellular embryos. The conclusion that differential protein levels do not explain the phenotype (C109) is well-supported.

result: Two other formin-related genes (inft-2 and frl-1) are expressed at the four-cell stage, but none are significantly over-expressed in EMS or P2 relative to ABa/ABp. Individual RNAi depletion of six other formin-related proteins did not decrease cytokinesis failure frequency in any blastomere in formincyk-1(ts) mutants, suggesting no single formin compensates for forminCYK-1 loss.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by transcriptional data citations and RNAi screen results (Figure 3—supplement 1). The negative results from the RNAi screen are appropriately interpreted as ruling out single formin compensation. The caveat that multiple formins might function together (C104) is appropriately acknowledged as speculation that cannot be ruled out by the data.

result: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly, suggesting use of a sub-optimal contractile ring. MyosinNMY-2 remains essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' actomyosin contractile ring likely drives division, albeit with substantially weakened F-actin.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by kinetic analysis of ring constriction (Figure 2—supplement 1) and the myosin-II requirement data (Figure 1). The slower constriction in formincyk-1(ts) EMS/P2 cells supports the sub-optimal ring interpretation (C164). The continued requirement for myosin-II (C165) is strong evidence that an actomyosin ring still drives division (C166). The overall conclusion (C167) is well-supported by the combined data.

result: Both cell-intrinsic (P2) and cell-extrinsic (EMS) mechanisms control cytokinetic variation in individual cell types and can protect against division failure when the contractile ring is weakened. This work establishes the C. elegans four-cell embryo as a system to study cytokinetic diversity.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C65, C153, and C161 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple experimental approaches. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from temperature-shift experiments, F-actin imaging, blastomere isolation/pairing, and SrcSRC-1 depletion. The establishment of the four-cell embryo as a model system is justified by the comprehensive characterization presented.

result: Background claims establishing that cytokinesis is powered by actomyosin ring constriction, that cytokinetic regulation has more diversity than previously appreciated, and that organism-wide mutations in cytokinesis genes cause cell-type-specific division defects in multiple organisms including humans.
evaluation: Claims C1-C28 represent established knowledge and literature review supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made, though verification of specific citation accuracy would require checking the original sources.

result: Background on C. elegans development and the four-cell embryo system, including cell lineage patterns, cell fate specification pathways, and the technical advantages of the system for studying cell-type-specific cytokinesis.
evaluation: Claims C29-C44 represent established knowledge about C. elegans development supported by appropriate citations to classic studies and reviews. These provide essential background for understanding the experimental system but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Description of the temperature-sensitive mutants used: myosin-IInmy-2(ts) has a mutation in the neck domain affecting dimerization, while formincyk-1(ts) has a mutation in the FH2 domain affecting F-actin polymerization. Both mutations completely block cytokinesis in one-cell embryos at 26°C with null-like phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 and C66-C69 describe the experimental tools used, supported by citations to previous characterization studies (Davies et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2010). The characterization of these mutants as having null-like phenotypes at restrictive temperature is important for interpreting the results and is appropriately cited.

result: Background on formin function: diaphanous family formins are thought essential for contractile ring assembly and constriction. ForminCYK-1 is the only worm diaphanous family formin. In formincyk-1(ts) one-cell embryos, F-actin is present at 16°C but not visible at 26°C when cytokinesis fails.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide background on formin function and characterization of the formincyk-1(ts) mutant, supported by citations and data from Figure 1—supplement 1. This establishes the basis for using forminCYK-1 inactivation to study F-actin-dependent cytokinesis.

result: Discussion of potential mechanisms: EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically while ABa/ABp divide symmetrically. PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis in one-cell embryos and localize asymmetrically in P2 but not obviously in EMS. PAR-6 RNAi eliminates cytokinetic protection in EMS/P2 but also disrupts normal cell fate specification.
evaluation: Claims C168-C173 discuss potential mechanisms involving cell polarity. While the PAR-6 RNAi data (Figure 8—supplement 2) show loss of protection, the authors appropriately note that this result is confounded by loss of normal cell fate specification (C173), making it impossible to distinguish specific roles for PAR proteins in cytokinesis from indirect effects. The discussion is appropriately cautious but the mechanism remains unclear.

result: Discussion of potential mechanisms including cytofission, polar cortical relaxation, and cell fate signaling pathways (Wnt/Frizzled and RTK/Src). The authors note that cytofission is unlikely, discuss polar relaxation as a possibility, and present evidence linking cell fate signaling to cytokinetic protection.
evaluation: Claims C174-C186 represent discussion and speculation about mechanisms. The dismissal of cytofission (C175) is supported by observations. The discussion of polar cortical relaxation (C176-C177) is speculative. The discussion of cell fate signaling (C178-C186) is supported by the correlation data and literature, but direct mechanistic evidence is limited. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation rather than established findings.

result: Discussion of potential evolutionary advantages: P2 is in the germline lineage and inherits distinct factors. EMS and P2 are upstream of founder cell formation and undergo asymmetric divisions, potentially explaining why these cells have extra protection to ensure successful division and proper lineage specification.
evaluation: Claims C187-C197 present speculative evolutionary explanations for the observed cytokinetic protection in EMS and P2. While the observations about lineage position and asymmetric division are factual (supported by established knowledge), the speculation about selective pressure and evolutionary advantage (C195, C197) represents reasonable hypotheses but lacks direct experimental support.

result: Prediction that similar regulation may contribute to cytokinetic variation in human cells and potentially mediate cell-type-specific pathologies, based on similarities between worm and human cell fate signaling and cytokinetic machinery.
evaluation: Claims C198-C199 represent speculative predictions about potential relevance to human biology. While the prediction is reasonable given the conservation of cytokinetic machinery and cell fate signaling pathways, it remains speculative without direct evidence in mammalian systems. This represents an appropriate discussion of potential broader implications.

result: Assumption that a 'normal' although F-actin-poor contractile ring still forms in EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully in formincyk-1(ts) embryos at restrictive temperature, despite inability to detect enriched F-actin.
evaluation: Claim C162 represents an assumption about what is happening in cells where F-actin cannot be detected but division succeeds. The authors acknowledge this is an assumption based on the observation that cells divide successfully. While reasonable given the myosin-II requirement, this remains an inference about undetectable structures rather than a directly supported observation.
